patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Gerald Hamill is a 55-year-old right-handed man with a history of post-traumatic splenectomy, hypogammaglobulinemia, and hypertension who presents to the emergency department brought by his wife after progressive confusion and worsening headache over the past 24 hours. His wife reports that he developed a sore throat and mild cough approximately four days ago and was seen by his primary care physician two days prior to presentation, at which time he was diagnosed with a presumed upper respiratory tract infection and started on oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily. He initially seemed to improve slightly, but yesterday morning he began complaining of a severe diffuse headache that he described as the worst headache of his life. He took acetaminophen with minimal relief. By yesterday evening, his wife noticed he was becoming increasingly drowsy and was not making sense in conversation, intermittently confusing the names of their grandchildren and asking repetitive questions. She checked his temperature overnight and recorded 38.9 degrees Celsius at approximately 02:00 this morning. He developed rigors and was shaking in bed. She also noted that he seemed to be wincing when she turned on the bedroom light, pulling the blankets over his head. By this morning, he was difficult to fully rouse and she became alarmed and called emergency services. On arrival, paramedics found him lethargic with a GCS of 12. In the emergency department, he intermittently opens his eyes to voice and can state his name but is confused about his location and the date. He complains of severe neck pain and photophobia when asked. He denies any recent travel, sick contacts beyond his initial URI symptoms, or trauma. His wife confirms he has not received pneumococcal or meningococcal vaccinations despite his asplenic status, something their primary care physician had discussed but they had not yet followed up on. She also recalls his previous episode of pneumococcal pneumonia three years ago that required hospitalization.

results.title: Dexamethasone in Adults with Bacterial Meningitis
results.authors: de Gans J, van de Beek D
results.key_finding: Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h x 4 days, given before or with the first dose of antibiotics) reduced unfavorable outcomes and mortality in adults with bacterial meningitis, particularly pneumococcal meningitis.

results.title: Community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults — ESCMID guideline
results.authors: van de Beek D, Cabellos C, et al.
results.key_finding: Strong recommendation for dexamethasone 10 mg IV q6h for 4 days in suspected bacterial meningitis in high-income countries, initiated before or with the first dose of antibiotics. Benefit most clearly demonstrated for pneumococcal meningitis.

results.title: IDSA Practice Guidelines for Bacterial Meningitis
results.authors: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, et al.
results.key_finding: Adjunctive dexamethasone recommended for adults with suspected pneumococcal meningitis, administered 10-20 minutes before or with the first dose of antibiotics. If given after antibiotics have been started, benefit is uncertain but IDSA still suggests administration.

output.summary: Adjunctive dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg or 10 mg IV every 6 hours for 4 days) has been shown in randomized controlled trials to reduce mortality and unfavorable outcomes in adult bacterial meningitis, with the greatest benefit demonstrated in pneumococcal meningitis (de Gans et al., NEJM 2002; mortality reduced from approximately 34% to 14%). The benefit is maximized when dexamethasone is administered before or with the first dose of antibiotics. In cases of prior antibiotic exposure, the evidence for timing is less clear; guidelines generally still recommend its use. Dexamethasone discontinuation may be considered when a non-pneumococcal organism is identified, as benefit has not been established for other pathogens.

sequence_constraints.reason: Per IDSA 2004, non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture whenever any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal neurological deficit, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60). LP performed in undetected mass effect can precipitate fatal herniation.

Blood cultures must be drawn (under interpret_labs) before the first dose of empiric antibiotics so that culture yield is not lost; in practice this means peripheral cultures are collected at the same draw as the CSF analysis is initiated, and the lab tube sequencing prevents antibiotic exposure before specimen acquisition.

critical_actions: Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or imaging beyond what is strictly needed for safety.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days in confirmed pneumococcal meningitis.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, or age >60).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.
Reassess and de-escalate antibiotics based on Gram stain, culture, and susceptibility results.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Recognise functional asplenia and ensure coverage of encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae); arrange post-recovery vaccination per ACIP.
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
key_reasoning_points: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotic timing matters: every hour of delay after the first hour increases mortality. Antibiotics MUST precede imaging or LP if either would delay treatment >60 minutes.
CT before LP is mandated when any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal signs, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60).
Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h × 4 days) given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
A negative CSF Gram stain (sensitivity ~60-90%, lower if antibiotic pretreated) does not exclude bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR or antigen testing retains sensitivity.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis.
Empiric coverage must include vancomycin + ceftriaxone in adults; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage if age >50 or immunocompromised.

Asplenia (anatomic or functional) dramatically increases risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae); these patients require lifelong vaccination and a low threshold for empiric antibiotics.
